Lecture 30

First-order PDEs and characteristics

We solve linear first-order equations along characteristic curves and prove existence and uniqueness for transport with decay and a source, at a constant and at a variable speed. We prove that data on a noncharacteristic curve determine a solution near each of its points.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Solve a linear first-order Cauchy problem along its characteristics, and verify the equation and the data.
  • Write the solution of transport with decay and a source by Duhamel’s formula, and find which part of the source reaches a given point.
  • Distinguish the value of a tracer from a conserved amount.
  • Test a data curve for being noncharacteristic, and explain how data on a characteristic lose existence or uniqueness.

Lecture 29 derived partial differential equations from balance laws. In this lecture we solve the linear equations of first order. Such an equation prescribes the rate of change of the unknown along one direction at each point. Along the curves that follow this direction, the characteristic curves, it becomes an ordinary differential equation of Lectures 4 and 5.

30.1 Transport at a constant speed

All equations of this lecture before Section 30.4 have the evolution form ut+a(x,t) ux+γ(x,t) u=f(x,t),u_t+a(x,t)\,u_x+\gamma(x,t)\,u=f(x,t),ut​+a(x,t)ux​+γ(x,t)u=f(x,t),(30.1) with an advection speed aaa, a decay rate γ\gammaγ (negative values mean growth) and a source fff, all real functions.

ut+a(x,t) ux+γ(x,t) u=f(x,t),u_t+a(x,t)\,u_x+\gamma(x,t)\,u=f(x,t),ut​+a(x,t)ux​+γ(x,t)u=f(x,t),(30.1)

Definition 30.1 (Cauchy problem and classical solution). Let aaa, γ\gammaγ and fff be continuous on R×[0,∞)\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), and let u0∈C1(R)u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R). A classical solution of the Cauchy problem for (30.1) with the initial data u0u_0u0​ is a function uuu that is continuous on R×[0,∞)\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), has continuous first partial derivatives on R×(0,∞)\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), satisfies (30.1) at every point of R×(0,∞)\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), and satisfies u(x,0)=u0(x)for every x∈R.u(x,0)=u_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\R .u(x,0)=u0​(x)for every x∈R.(30.2)

The equation is required only for t>0t>0t>0, and the data are reached by continuity. This is Lecture 29’s notion of a classical solution, for an equation of first order.

30.2 Transport with decay and a source

Many substances are carried by a flow and decay at the same time: a radioactive isotope, a reacting chemical, or bacteria in a river. Suppose that the substance decays at the constant rate γ≥0\gamma\ge0γ≥0, so that the amount γu ⁣dx\gamma u\dd xγudx is lost per unit time in a short interval of length  ⁣dx\dd xdx, and that it is added at the rate f(x,t)f(x,t)f(x,t) per unit length and unit time. The balance on [x1,x2][x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​] gains the term ∫x1x2(f−γu) ⁣dx\int_{x_1}^{x_2}(f-\gamma u)\dd x∫x1​x2​​(f−γu)dx on the right, and the localization gives ut+aux+γu=f(x,t),u_t+au_x+\gamma u=f(x,t),ut​+aux​+γu=f(x,t),(30.6) the evolution form (30.1) with constant aaa and γ\gammaγ.

ut+aux+γu=f(x,t),u_t+au_x+\gamma u=f(x,t),ut​+aux​+γu=f(x,t),(30.6)

30.3 Variable speed

When the speed of the flow changes with the position or the time, the characteristics are no longer straight lines. Their slopes are prescribed instead by an ordinary differential equation.

Definition 30.7 (Characteristic curves). Let aaa have continuous first partial derivatives on R2\R^2R2. A characteristic curve of (30.1) is the graph {(X(t),t)}\{(X(t),t)\}{(X(t),t)} of a maximal solution XXX (Lecture 4) of the characteristic equation  ⁣dX ⁣dt=a(X,t).\frac{\dd X}{\dd t}=a(X,t).dtdX​=a(X,t).(30.13)

Along a characteristic the chain rule gives  ⁣d ⁣dt u(X(t),t)=ux(X(t),t) a(X(t),t)+ut(X(t),t),\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\,u(X(t),t)=u_x(X(t),t)\,a(X(t),t)+u_t(X(t),t),dtd​u(X(t),t)=ux​(X(t),t)a(X(t),t)+ut​(X(t),t),(30.14) so (30.1) becomes the linear equation U′+γ(X(t),t)U=f(X(t),t)U'+\gamma(X(t),t)U=f(X(t),t)U′+γ(X(t),t)U=f(X(t),t) for U(t)=u(X(t),t)U(t)=u(X(t),t)U(t)=u(X(t),t). By Lecture 4’s existence theorem, with the Lipschitz condition from its lemma on continuous derivatives, exactly one characteristic passes through each point, and by its consequence on disjoint graphs two distinct characteristics never meet.

Lemma 30.8 (Flows of planar systems · cited). Let V\vv VV be a map from an open set U⊂R2U\subset\R^2U⊂R2 to R2\R^2R2 with continuous first partial derivatives. The next example compares the two forms for one flow.

30.4 Data on a curve

So far the data were given on the line t=0t=0t=0. We now give them on a curve in a plane with the coordinates (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), and ask when they determine a solution. The general linear equation of first order in two variables is a(x,y) ux+b(x,y) uy+γ(x,y) u=f(x,y)((x,y)∈U),a(x,y)\,u_x+b(x,y)\,u_y+\gamma(x,y)\,u=f(x,y)\qquad\bigl((x,y)\in U\bigr),a(x,y)ux​+b(x,y)uy​+γ(x,y)u=f(x,y)((x,y)∈U),(30.18) on an open set U⊂R2U\subset\R^2U⊂R2, where aaa, bbb, γ\gammaγ and fff have continuous first partial derivatives and (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\ne(0,0)(a,b)=(0,0) at every point of UUU. The evolution form (30.1) is the case y=ty=ty=t and b=1b=1b=1. The characteristic curves of (30.18) are the solutions of the autonomous system  ⁣dx ⁣dμ=a(x,y), ⁣dy ⁣dμ=b(x,y),\frac{\dd x}{\dd\mu}=a(x,y),\qquad\frac{\dd y}{\dd\mu}=b(x,y),dμdx​=a(x,y),dμdy​=b(x,y),(30.19) with a parameter μ\muμ that need not be a time. Along such a curve  ⁣du(x(μ),y(μ))/ ⁣dμ=aux+buy\dd u(x(\mu),y(\mu))/\dd\mu=au_x+bu_ydu(x(μ),y(μ))/dμ=aux​+buy​, by the chain rule. So on the curve (30.18) becomes  ⁣du ⁣dμ=f−γu,\frac{\dd u}{\dd\mu}=f-\gamma u ,dμdu​=f−γu, a third equation coupled to (30.19).

The data are given on a curve ξ↦(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))\xi\mapsto(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi))ξ↦(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ)) in UUU, ξ∈J\xi\in Jξ∈J, an open interval, with continuous derivatives and with (x0′,y0′)≠(0,0)(x_0',y_0')\ne(0,0)(x0′​,y0′​)=(0,0): u(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))=u0(ξ)(ξ∈J),u\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)=u_0(\xi)\qquad(\xi\in J),u(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))=u0​(ξ)(ξ∈J),(30.20) with u0∈C1(J)u_0\in C^1(J)u0​∈C1(J). Suppose that a solution with continuous first derivatives exists near the curve. Differentiating the data along the curve, and evaluating the equation on it, gives two linear equations for the two values uxu_xux​ and uyu_yuy​ at a point of the curve: x0′(ξ) ux+y0′(ξ) uy=u0′(ξ),a ux+b uy=f−γu0(ξ),x_0'(\xi)\,u_x+y_0'(\xi)\,u_y=u_0'(\xi),\qquad a\,u_x+b\,u_y=f-\gamma u_0(\xi),x0′​(ξ)ux​+y0′​(ξ)uy​=u0′​(ξ),aux​+buy​=f−γu0​(ξ), with aaa, bbb, γ\gammaγ and fff evaluated at (x0(ξ),y0(ξ))(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi))(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ)). The determinant of this system decides whether the data and the equation fix the gradient on the curve.

Definition 30.11 (Noncharacteristic data). The data curve is noncharacteristic at ξ\xiξ if Δ(ξ)=x0′(ξ) b(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))−y0′(ξ) a(x0(ξ),y0(ξ))≠0.\Delta(\xi)=x_0'(\xi)\,b\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)-y_0'(\xi)\,a\bigl(x_0(\xi),y_0(\xi)\bigr)\ne0 .Δ(ξ)=x0′​(ξ)b(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))−y0′​(ξ)a(x0​(ξ),y0​(ξ))=0.(30.21)

The number Δ(ξ)\Delta(\xi)Δ(ξ) is the determinant of the matrix with the rows (x0′,y0′)(x_0',y_0')(x0′​,y0′​) and (a,b)(a,b)(a,b). It is nonzero exactly when the tangent (x0′,y0′)(x_0',y_0')(x0′​,y0′​) is not parallel to the characteristic direction (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), that is, when the curve is not tangent to the characteristic through that point. The proposition is local: it gives a solution in a neighbourhood of one point of the curve. Theorem 30.9 is a global version for the line t=0t=0t=0, made possible by the linear bound on the speed. The next example shows what goes wrong when Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0.

Example 30.13 (Data on a characteristic). We show that data on a characteristic can rule out every solution, or allow infinitely many. For ut+aux=0u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0 with a constant aaa, give the data on the characteristic x=atx=atx=at: u(at,t)=u0(t)(t∈R).u(at,t)=u_0(t)\qquad(t\in\R).u(at,t)=u0​(t)(t∈R). In the coordinates (x,y)=(x,t)(x,y)=(x,t)(x,y)=(x,t) the curve is x0(ξ)=aξx_0(\xi)=a\xix0​(ξ)=aξ and y0(ξ)=ξy_0(\xi)=\xiy0​(ξ)=ξ, and (30.21) with b=1b=1b=1 gives Δ=a⋅1−1⋅a=0\Delta=a\cdot1-1\cdot a=0Δ=a⋅1−1⋅a=0 at every point (Figure 30.3). By the argument of Proposition 30.2, every solution on R2\R^2R2 with continuous first partial derivatives is constant on each characteristic, so it is u(x,t)=F(x−at)u(x,t)=F(x-at)u(x,t)=F(x−at) with F(ξ)=u(ξ,0)F(\xi)=u(\xi,0)F(ξ)=u(ξ,0) and F∈C1(R)F\in C^1(\R)F∈C1(R). Data on a characteristic say nothing about the other characteristics, and they must themselves satisfy the equation along the curve. ◃

30.5 The method and its second-order counterpart

The method of characteristics consists of the following steps.

  • Check that the data curve is noncharacteristic, Δ≠0\Delta\ne0Δ=0.

  • Solve the characteristic system from the data curve.

  • Solve  ⁣du/ ⁣dμ=f−γu\dd u/\dd\mu=f-\gamma udu/dμ=f−γu along each characteristic, with the data at its foot.

  • Check the equation, the data and the region the characteristics cover.

For an equation of first order, data on a noncharacteristic curve, together with the equation, determine the gradient of uuu on the curve. An equation of second order needs the values of uuu and of its derivative across the curve, the Cauchy data on a curve of Lecture 29, which on the line t=0t=0t=0 are uuu and utu_tut​. Its characteristic curves are the curves along which these data and the equation fail to determine the second derivatives of uuu. Lecture 31 finds them for the wave equation utt=c2uxxu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}utt​=c2uxx​, with the wave speed ccc of Lecture 29. They are the lines x±ct=constx\pm ct=\text{const}x±ct=const, two families instead of one, as Lecture 29’s classification of hyperbolic equations suggests.

Summary

A linear first-order equation prescribes the rate of change of uuu along the direction (a,b)(a,b)(a,b). Along the characteristic curves it becomes the linear ODE  ⁣du/ ⁣dμ=f−γu\dd u/\dd\mu=f-\gamma udu/dμ=f−γu. The Cauchy problem has exactly one classical solution, the initial value at the foot carried along the characteristic, damped, plus the source collected along it: by Duhamel’s formula for a constant speed, and with characteristics from an ODE for a speed with a linear bound. Data on a curve determine a solution near every point where the curve is noncharacteristic. Data on a characteristic can rule out every solution or leave it undetermined.

  • Characteristics: for ut+a(x,t)ux+γu=fu_t+a(x,t)u_x+\gamma u=fut​+a(x,t)ux​+γu=f, the curves  ⁣dX/ ⁣dt=a(X,t)\dd X/\dd t=a(X,t)dX/dt=a(X,t). Along them  ⁣du/ ⁣dt=f−γu\dd u/\dd t=f-\gamma udu/dt=f−γu. The foot of the characteristic through (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) is Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t).

  • Duhamel’s formula: for constant aaa and γ\gammaγ, u0∈C1(R)u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R), fff and fxf_xfx​ continuous, u=e−γtu0(x−at)+∫0te−γ(t−τ)f(x−a(t−τ),τ) ⁣dτu=\ee^{-\gamma t}u_0(x-at)+\int_0^t\ee^{-\gamma(t-\tau)}f(x-a(t-\tau),\tau)\dd\tauu=e−γtu0​(x−at)+∫0t​e−γ(t−τ)f(x−a(t−τ),τ)dτ is the unique classical solution.

  • Variable speed: for aaa, γ\gammaγ, fff with continuous first derivatives, ∣a∣≤A0+A1∣x∣\abs a\le A_0+A_1\abs x∣a∣≤A0​+A1​∣x∣ and u0∈C1(R)u_0\in C^1(\R)u0​∈C1(R), the Cauchy problem has exactly one classical solution: the initial value at the foot Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t)Y(0;x,t), damped by e−P(0;x,t)\ee^{-P(0;x,t)}e−P(0;x,t), plus ∫0te−P(τ;x,t)f(Y(τ;x,t),τ) ⁣dτ\int_0^t\ee^{-P(\tau;x,t)}f(Y(\tau;x,t),\tau)\dd\tau∫0t​e−P(τ;x,t)f(Y(τ;x,t),τ)dτ.

  • Conservation form: ut+(au)x=0u_t+(au)_x=0ut​+(au)x​=0, that is, γ=ax\gamma=a_xγ=ax​, describes an amount, as in Example 30.10. The form ut+aux=0u_t+au_x=0ut​+aux​=0 keeps the value carried by each particle.

  • Noncharacteristic data: for coefficients, curve and data with continuous first derivatives, Δ=x0′b−y0′a≠0\Delta=x_0'b-y_0'a\ne0Δ=x0′​b−y0′​a=0 at a point of the data curve gives exactly one solution near that point. Data on a characteristic determine nothing off it and must be compatible along it.

Lecture 31 finds the characteristics of the wave equation and solves the vibrating string on the whole line.
